prompt: Why is a custom scheme such as planner:// a weak way to reach your app?

choices.text: It only works on Android
choices.why: Both platforms support custom schemes.

choices.text: It needs a file on a website before it works
choices.why: That is a verified link; a custom scheme needs nothing on the web.

choices.text: Any other app is free to claim it too
choices.why: Right. Nothing checks the claim, so a link the planner sends ends up in somebody else's app.

choices.text: The system refuses schemes that are not registered with the store
choices.why: No store registers schemes; that is the problem, not the protection.

prompt: What makes an https link a verified one, on both platforms?

choices.text: A file on that website names the app, and the system checks it
choices.why: Right. Only whoever controls the domain can put the file there.

choices.text: The link uses a reverse-DNS name
choices.why: Apple's documentation says a reverse-DNS scheme name prevents nothing.

choices.text: The app was approved by the store's review
choices.why: Review does not verify a domain; the website does.

choices.text: The link carries a secret token
choices.why: Nothing in the link is secret; the proof is on the site.

prompt: On Android 12, an app declares https://planner.example.com in its manifest, but the site has no valid file. What does a tap on the link do?

choices.text: Opens the app, since the manifest names the domain
choices.why: From Android 12 a web intent reaches an app only if it is approved for the domain.

choices.text: Asks the user which app to use, every time
choices.why: On Android 12 and later an unverified web link opens the default browser.

choices.text: Shows an error saying the file is missing
choices.why: Nobody is told; the link just goes to the browser.

choices.text: Opens the browser
choices.why: Right. Unverified, the app is treated as if it never asked.

prompt: Match each name to what it is.

pairs.right: asks Android to check the site

right_distractors: a custom scheme the store registers

prompt: A message app wants to steal the planner's links. Which kind of planner link can it intercept, and why?

choices.text: The https ones, by declaring the same domain in its manifest
choices.why: Declaring is not enough; the site's file names only the planner.

choices.text: planner:// ones, since claiming a scheme is never checked
choices.why: Right. The https links need the site's file, which only the planner's owner controls.

choices.text: Neither: the system blocks a second app from declaring either kind
choices.why: Nothing blocks declaring a custom scheme.

choices.text: Both, as long as it is installed first
choices.why: Order of installation does not verify a domain.

prompt: What does Apple's documentation on custom URL schemes ask an app to do with every link it receives?

choices.text: Open it at once, since the system already checked it
choices.why: The system checks nothing about a custom scheme link's content.

choices.text: Validate it, discard it if malformed, and let it do nothing risky
choices.why: Right. A link is input from outside, whoever wrote it.

choices.text: Send it to the website to be checked
choices.why: No; the app validates it itself.

choices.text: Ask the user to confirm each one
choices.why: The documentation asks for validation, not a confirmation dialog.

prompt: Why does follow.ts refuse http://planner.example.com/course/sql?

choices.text: The course sql does not exist
choices.why: The same course opens through the https link.

choices.text: Node.js cannot parse a URL that starts with http, only https
choices.why: It parses them; the parser chooses to refuse.

choices.text: The path has too many parts
choices.why: course/sql has exactly two.

choices.text: It is http, and a verified link is always https
choices.why: Right. parts accepts only planner: and https on the planner's host.

prompt: In planner://course/sql, where does Node's URL parser put the word course?

choices.text: In the host
choices.why: Right, which is why parts puts url.host back at the front of the list.

choices.text: In the protocol
choices.why: The protocol is planner:.

choices.text: In the pathname
choices.why: The pathname is /sql; course is read as the host.

choices.text: Nowhere: it is dropped
choices.why: It is kept, as the host.

prompt: planner://course/sql/delete is refused. What rule does that enforce?

choices.text: Course ids may not contain the word delete
choices.why: No word list is involved; the path has one part too many.

choices.text: Custom schemes cannot have three parts
choices.why: The https spelling with three parts is refused too.

choices.text: A link opens a screen and asks for nothing more
choices.why: Right. A known screen with an extra part is still refused.

choices.text: Deleting a course needs the user to be signed in
choices.why: The planner has no accounts, and no link may delete anything.

prompt: Of the ten links in follow.ts, how many does the planner open?
A link to one course opens with courses under course:sql on the stack. What does the student gain?

choices.text: Back and up land on the list, inside the app, as if they had tapped there
choices.why: Right. It is the synthetic back stack Android's navigation principles ask for.

choices.text: The link is verified twice
choices.why: Verification is the system's, not the stack's.

choices.text: Nothing; it behaves exactly the same as opening course:sql on its own, with no list
choices.why: Alone, the first back press would leave the app.

choices.text: The list loads faster later
choices.why: Speed is not the point; the stack is.

prompt: planner://course/SQL Databases is refused because a link names a course by its ___, never by its title.
Which of these does a platform check when it fetches the association file? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the status is 200
choices.why: Right; a 404 is no file.

choices.text: there is no redirect
choices.why: Right; both platforms' documentation says so.

choices.text: Content-Type is application/json, which Android's documentation requires
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: the server sends a Date header
choices.why: site.ts turns Date off so runs repeat; no platform asks for it.

prompt: What in assetlinks.json stops another app that copies the planner's package name?

choices.text: The file's location under /.well-known/
choices.why: The location is the same for every site.

choices.text: The relation delegate_permission/common.handle_all_urls
choices.why: Every statement carries that relation; it names the permission, not the app.

choices.text: The certificate fingerprint
choices.why: Right. The copy cannot be signed with the planner's key.

choices.text: The namespace android_app
choices.why: That only says the target is an Android app.

prompt: A site sends every request for /.well-known/apple-app-site-association to www. with a 301, and the file there is perfect. Do universal links work?

choices.text: Yes, because the redirect lands on a valid file
choices.why: The file must be served without a redirect; following one is not allowed.

choices.text: No: a redirect counts as no file
choices.why: Right. Apple's documentation asks for https, a valid certificate and no redirects.

choices.text: Only on iOS 14 and later
choices.why: The CDN changes who fetches the file, not the rule about redirects.

choices.text: Yes, if the team id is a real one
choices.why: A real team id does not excuse a redirect.

prompt: Since iOS 14, where does an iPhone get a site's apple-app-site-association file from?

choices.text: Straight from the site, each time a link is tapped
choices.why: Not on each tap, and not from the site directly.

choices.text: From inside the app's bundle, beside its other files
choices.why: The app carries the entitlement; the file lives on the web.

choices.text: From the App Store listing
choices.why: The listing does not carry it.

choices.text: From a content delivery network Apple runs
choices.why: Right, which fetched it from the site.

prompt: Is it a problem that anybody can read a site's assetlinks.json?

choices.text: Yes: it leaks the signing key
choices.why: It holds a fingerprint of the certificate, not the key.

choices.text: Yes, so it should sit behind a login
choices.why: Behind a login the platforms could not fetch it.

choices.text: No: it is public by design, and nothing in it is a secret
choices.why: Right. It says which apps the site vouches for, and that may be known.

choices.text: Only if it lists more than one app
choices.why: The number of apps changes nothing.

prompt: The planner is not installed, and a friend's link https://planner.example.com/course/sql is tapped. What opens?

choices.text: The browser, and the website's page about that course
choices.why: Right. A verified link is an ordinary web address.

choices.text: The store, on the planner's page
choices.why: The system does not send a link to the store by itself.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: That is the custom scheme's fate, not the https link's.

choices.text: An error asking to install the planner first
choices.why: No error; the browser takes the address.

prompt: A person is reading planner.example.com in Safari and taps a link to another page of the same site. Where does it open?

choices.text: In the App Store
choices.why: The store is not involved.

choices.text: In the planner, if it is installed and verified
choices.why: That is what happens from a different domain.

choices.text: In a dialog asking which to use
choices.why: iOS shows no such dialog for universal links.

choices.text: In Safari
choices.why: Right. Apple keeps a same-domain tap in the browser, assuming the person meant to keep browsing.

prompt: Why is a deferred deep link harder than an ordinary one?

choices.text: Because the store refuses links with paths
choices.why: The store page opens; the link's screen is what is lost.

choices.text: An install is not a link being opened, so the link is lost on the way
choices.why: Right. Carrying it across needs a referrer, or some other way of matching the install to the tap.

choices.text: Because it uses a custom scheme
choices.why: Deferral is about the install, whatever the scheme.

choices.text: Because it needs both files on the website
choices.why: The files verify links; they do not survive an install for you.

prompt: Put the system's questions about a tapped https link in the order it asks them, ending with the outcome when both answers are no.
items: is an installed app verified for this domain?

prompt: The planner team adds /week to the parser but forgets it in the AASA components. What happens on an iPhone with the planner installed?

choices.text: The planner opens on the week, since the parser accepts it
choices.why: The system decides before the parser runs; the file does not list /week.

choices.text: The browser opens the week's web page
choices.why: Right. Only the paths in components open the app.

choices.text: The link is refused with an error
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; it simply goes to the web.

choices.text: Every planner link stops working
choices.why: The other components still match.

prompt: Match each link to what follow.ts printed for it.
A team wants to keep its planner:// links and drop the website. What does it give up?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the parser is strict
choices.why: A strict parser does not stop another app claiming the scheme, nor help a phone without the app.

choices.text: Only the back stack that toNav puts under the course screen
choices.why: toNav builds that stack for either kind of link.

choices.text: The ability to open the app from a chat
choices.why: A custom scheme opens it from a chat, when nobody else claims the scheme.

choices.text: Links that only it answers, and a page for people without the app
choices.why: Right. Those are the two things a verified link adds.

prompt: Which part of opening a link is the app's own code, rather than the system's?

choices.text: Turning the URL into a screen, or refusing it
choices.why: Right. That is parse and toNav.

choices.text: Fetching the association file
choices.why: The system fetches it at install.

choices.text: Deciding whether the app or the browser opens
choices.why: The system decides that, before the app runs.

choices.text: Checking the certificate fingerprint
choices.why: The system compares it with the app's signature.
